items.text: Denmark states that it has serious disagreements with the United States regarding the future of Greenland. US President Donald Trump says the US needs full control of Greenland for national security and missile defense. Danish and Greenland leaders say this is unacceptable, but they remain open to cooperation on defense and security as allies. They say ownership of Greenland is not for discussion. Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. The US has had military bases there for many years, but Denmark controls the land. Trump argues Greenland is important to block Russia and China in the Arctic. Denmark has promised to increase its own military presence, but Trump says this may not be enough. Talks between the US, Denmark, and Greenland will continue; however, public support in the US for a takeover is very low. Trump has also warned he may use trade tariffs against countries that oppose his plan. This has increased tension between allies and raised concerns about future cooperation. Difficult words: ownership (legal control of something), self-governing territory (a place that makes many of its own rules but still belongs to a larger country), oppose (to say no or act against something), tension (a difficult or stressed situation between people or countries). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Denmark and the United States disagree about Greenland. President Trump says the US needs Greenland for security and wants full control. Denmark and Greenland say no. They say they can work with the US on defense , but Greenland will not belong to the US. Greenland governs itself but stays part of Denmark. The US already has a military base there. Trump says Greenland helps protect the Arctic from Russia and China. Denmark plans to send more soldiers, but Trump says Denmark cannot protect Greenland on its own. The countries plan more talks, but many Americans don’t support a takeover . Trump also speaks about trade taxes on countries that say no. This situation causes worries in countries which support Greenland. Difficult words: defense (protection from danger or attack), govern (to control and make rules for a place or people), takeover (when one country or group takes control of another). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Denmark and the US argue about Greenland. President Trump says that the US needs Greenland for safety . Denmark and Greenland say no. They say that Greenland will stay with Denmark. Greenland is part of Denmark. But Denmark does not rule there. The US has soldiers in Denmark. Trump says that Greenland is important because of Russia and China. Denmark says that it will send more soldiers. The countries will talk again soon. Many people in the US do not want Greenland. Trump says that he may use trade rules to get what he wants. Countries which support Greenland may pay higher tariffs on US products. Difficult words: argue (to speak against someone), safety (a situation when everyone is safe), tariff (a tax on products which come into a country). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Elon Musk’s AI tool Grok will stop editing photos of real people to show them in revealing clothes in places where this is illegal. The decision follows strong public anger about sexual AI deepfakes that show people without their permission . X said it added new technical limits to block this use and said paid users are easier to identify and hold responsible. Regulators and campaign groups welcomed the move but said checks continue. The UK regulator Ofcom said its review of possible law-breaking still continues. In the United States, officials in California also began checks into sexual AI images, including cases that involve children. Some people affected said these fake images feel deeply harmful and very real. The case shows how hard it is to control new digital tools. Governments say tech companies must protect users, especially children. New laws aim to stop abuse before it spreads. Many experts believe this moment could shape future rules for AI tools on social media platforms. Difficult words: revealing (showing a lot of the body, especially in a sexual way), permission (saying yes or allowing someone to do something), regulator (an authority that controls rules). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Elon Musk’s AI tool Grok will stop changing photos of real people into sexual images in countries where this breaks the law. Many people complained about fake pictures that show women and children without permission . X says it adds tools to stop this and limits image editing to paid users. UK and US officials welcome the change but continue checks. UK authorities are still looking at possible law-breaking. In California, leaders also check the spread of sexual AI images. People affected say the pictures look real and cause serious harm. This case shows problems with new technology. Governments say tech companies must protect people online. New rules try to stop abuse early. Experts think this change could lead to stronger control of AI tools in the future. Difficult words: permission (saying yes or letting someone do something), limit (a rule that stops something from going too far), abuse (using someone in a bad or harmful way). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Elon Musk’s AI tool called Grok can no longer change photos of real people into sexual pictures. This will stop places where this is illegal . Many people feel angry and upset about fake images online. Some people say that the fake pictures look real and hurt them. The company puts limits on the tool. Only paying users can change photos now. Leaders in the UK and the US say that this is good news. Authorities still check if users do not break the rules. This story shows that new technology can cause problems. Governments want companies to keep people safe online. Many people think that new rules for AI will come soon. Difficult words: sexual (about sex or the body in an intimate way), illegal (against the rules), limit (a rule which stops something from going too far). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A SpaceX capsule left the International Space Station earlier than planned because one astronaut needed urgent medical care. The crew included two Americans, one Japanese astronaut, and one Russian cosmonaut. NASA didn’t share details about the medical condition to protect privacy . The capsule began its trip back to Earth after more than five months in space. The spacecraft started its return in the evening and headed toward the Pacific Ocean near California. The trip was expected to last about ten hours and included a very hot entry through Earth’s atmosphere. Live video showed the capsule slowly moving away from the space station while the crew sat inside wearing space suits. NASA said this was the first time it ended a space station mission early because of a health problem. Officials explained that doctors on Earth can give better care and checks. The mission commander said everyone was stable, but the return was the best choice. Another crew will arrive at the station later. Difficult words: urgent (needing quick action), privacy (keeping personal information secret), mission commander (the main leader of a space mission). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

A SpaceX spacecraft left the space station early because one astronaut had a serious health problem. The crew had four people from the United States, Japan, and Russia. NASA didn’t say who was sick because it wanted to protect the person. The crew stayed in space for about five months before the return. The capsule left the station in the evening and flew back to Earth. It traveled for about ten hours and landed in the ocean near California. Cameras showed the spacecraft moving away while the astronauts sat inside in space suits. NASA said this was the first time it ended a mission early for health reasons. Doctors on Earth can check the astronaut better. The crew leader said everyone felt fine, but the early return was the right thing to do. Difficult words: crew (a group of people who work together on a ship or spacecraft), protect (to keep someone or something safe), capsule (a small spacecraft). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A SpaceX capsule leaves the space station early. One astronaut has a health problem. He needs help on Earth. Four people travel together in the spacecraft . They come from the United States, Japan, and Russia. NASA does not say who feels sick. The capsule moves away from the station and flies back to Earth. The trip takes many hours. The capsule lands in the ocean near California. The astronauts wear space suits inside. NASA says that this is the first early return because of health problems. Doctors on Earth can help more. Another group of astronauts comes to the station. Difficult words: capsule (a small spacecraft that carries people), spacecraft (a vehicle which travels in space), health (how well a person’s body and mind are doing). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Global temperatures in 2025 were slightly lower than in 2024 because of La Niña, a natural weather pattern that cools the Pacific Ocean. Even so, 2025 became the third warmest year ever recorded. The last three years were the hottest in history, which shows a clear long-term warming trend. Scientists say today’s temperatures stay far above levels from before the heavy use of fossil fuels . Experts explain that this warming happens mainly because people continue to release carbon emissions. Although some cooling came from natural causes, it didn’t stop the overall rise. Scientists warn that more heat records and stronger weather events will follow if emissions don’t fall quickly. Fires, floods, and heat waves have already affected many parts of the world. Researchers say the science is very clear and not uncertain. Governments, companies, and individuals all play a role. People can vote, spend money carefully, and support cleaner energy. Reducing emissions soon can help slow warming and protect the planet. Difficult words: pattern (the way something happens again and again), fossil fuel (oil, gas, or coal that people burn to make energy). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

In 2025, global temperatures dropped a little compared to 2024 because of La Niña. Still, the year became the third hottest ever. Scientists say the world is much warmer than it was ten years ago. Human activity and carbon emissions keep heat in the air. Natural cooling doesn’t stop climate change. Experts warn that fires, floods, and heat waves grow stronger in a warmer world. No place stays safe from these changes. The last three years broke records and pushed the planet closer to climate limits. Scientists say the facts stay clear. Countries need to cut emissions faster. People can change things because they can vote, choose cleaner energy, and support responsible companies. Small actions together can help slow warming. Difficult words: drop (to become lower or less), emission (gas which houses, cars, and companies release into the air), responsible (when you do the right thing and care about the results). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The world stays very warm in 2025. The year is a little cooler than 2024, but it is still one of the hottest years ever. Scientists say that people cause this heat. They still use oil, gas, and coal . Warm weather brings big problems. Fires, floods, and strong heat happen more often. These events hurt people, animals, and nature. No country stays safe from climate change. Experts say that everyone can help. People can vote, save energy, and support clean energy. If many people do something, the planet can become safer in the future. Difficult words: cause (to make something happen), coal (a black rock that people burn to make energy), support (to help or stand behind someone or something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The Louvre Museum in Paris now asks visitors from outside Europe to pay a higher entry fee . The price for individual visitors rises from 22 euros to 32 euros. Museum leaders say this change helps pay for repairs and updates at the building. Similar higher prices will appear at other famous cultural places in France. This system uses dual pricing, which means people pay different prices based on where they come from. This idea is common in poorer countries but rare in Europe. Some visitors accept the higher price; however, others say it feels unfair and limits access to culture. Trade unions also say culture shouldn’t feel like a business product. The French government supports the change and says the museum needs more money for safety and renovation. The Louvre plans to use the extra income for long-term projects. Children under 18 and young Europeans can still enter for free, but debate about fairness continues. Difficult words: fee (money you pay for a service), dual (having two different parts or types), trade unions (a group that protects workers and their rights). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

The Louvre Museum in Paris now charges higher prices to visitors from outside Europe. The entry fee rises from 22 euros to 32 euros. The museum says it needs more money to fix and improve the building. Other French museums also plan similar price changes. This system uses dual pricing, which means people pay different prices based on where they live. Some tourists say the price feels fine, but others say it feels unfair. Some believe that culture should stay open to everyone and not become only a paid product. The government supports the plan and says the museum needs funds for safety and repairs. Children under 18 can still enter for free. People talk a lot about money and if it is fair to pay for culture. Difficult words: entry fee (money you pay to go inside a place), based on (decided by something), fund (money used to pay for something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The Louvre Museum in Paris asks some visitors to pay more money. People from outside Europe now pay 32 euros to enter . The museum says that it needs money to fix and care for the building. Other museums in France also plan higher prices. Some visitors say that the new price is okay. Other visitors say that it is not fair. They believe that culture should stay open to all people and not only rich visitors. The government says that the museum needs money. Children under 18 can enter for free. Many people still talk about what is fair. Difficult words: enter (to go inside), fix (to repair something), rich (when you have a lot of money). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A French writer, Bertrand Scholler, has been found guilty of cyberbullying the French president’s wife. He shared an edited photo online that mocked her body and spread false ideas about her gender and private life. A Paris court heard that these online posts caused serious harm to the president’s wife and her family. Her daughter spoke in court and described fear, stress, and shame. The false stories spread widely on social media and became harder to stop. The court decided that this behavior was bullying, not free speech or humor. The court gave Scholler a six-month suspended sentence. He was one of ten people found guilty in the same case, and he later said that he didn’t regret his actions. The case started a wider debate in France about online behavior and responsibility. Some people worry about limits on free speech; however, others say the ruling protects people from harm. The president’s wife said she wants to show young people that it is right to stand up against bullying. Difficult words: cyberbullying (using the internet to hurt or attack someone), mock (to laugh at someone in a mean way), ruling (an official decision made by a court). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

A French writer shared an edited photo of the president’s wife and wrote false stories about her online. He and nine other people went to court for cyberbullying , and the court found them guilty. The writer received a six-month suspended sentence and said he didn’t feel sorry. The Macron family explained how the posts caused pain and stress. The stories spread fast on social media and reached many people. The judge said these actions caused harm, and they were not a normal opinion or humor. Some people in France now worry about free speech , but many agree with stricter rules online. The president’s wife said she wants to help young people feel brave enough to speak out against bullying. Difficult words: edited (changed from the original), cyberbullying (using the internet to hurt or attack someone), free speech (the right to say what you think). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A French writer posts bad pictures and stories about the president’s wife online. He changes a photo and shares lies . A court in Paris says that this is wrong. The man does not go to prison, but he gets a six-month penalty . The Macron family feels sad and hurt. Many people see these posts. The stories spread fast on the internet and do not stop easily. The court says that this is bullying . It really hurts people. The story makes people talk about how to act online. The president’s wife wants to help young people speak out when bullying happens. It is important not to stay quiet. Difficult words: lie (something what is not true), penalty (what happens to you when you break a rule), bullying (when you are unkind to someone again and again). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Strong winds, snow, and freezing temperatures have hit large parts of western Europe after the arrival of Storm Goretti. Weather experts gave serious warnings in several countries. In southwest England, officials gave a rare red warning for wind, with speeds up to 160 kilometers per hour and dangerous conditions near the sea. In France, strong winds caused power cuts, and many homes lost electricity. In northern Germany, heavy snow and wind caused major problems. Some areas received up to 20 centimeters of snow, which disrupted schools, and many students stayed at home or learned online. Authorities asked people to avoid travel because roads and paths became unsafe. Workers used many vehicles to clear snow and spread salt to make roads safer. Train services in northern Germany ran less often, and airports warned of delays and cancellations. Some areas later received lighter warnings, but cold weather continued. Officials advised people to travel only when necessary and to stay careful during the storm. Difficult words: rare (not common, not happening often), disrupt (to stop something from working normally), avoid (to stay away from something). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Storm Goretti brought strong winds, snow, and freezing weather to western Europe. Weather services gave serious warnings . In southwest England, wind reached very high speeds and caused danger near the coast. In France, many homes lost electricity because strong winds damaged power lines. Northern Germany faced heavy snow and wind. Some places saw deep snow, and schools closed for safety. Officials told people not to travel unless necessary. Road workers cleared snow and added salt to reduce danger on streets and paths. Train companies reduced services, and airports warned travelers about delays and cancellations . Some areas later faced weaker warnings, but cold weather stayed. People needed to stay careful and plan their travel carefully. Difficult words: warning (a message which tells people about danger), unless (if not), cancellation (stopping something planned). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Strong winds, snow, and cold weather hit western Europe. A big storm causes problems in many places. In England, very strong wind makes the sea dangerous. In France, many homes have no power . In Germany, snow falls heavily in the north. Schools close, and people stay at home. Roads are not safe, so workers clean them and put salt on them. Trains run less, and planes are late. Officials tell people to stay safe and travel only a little. The cold weather continues. People must be careful. Difficult words: cause (to make something happen), power (electricity), plane (a vehicle which flies in the sky and takes people to another place). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A 37-year-old woman died after a shooting during an immigration raid in Minneapolis, US. Federal immigration officers stopped her car in the middle of a residential street and ordered her to get out. Video recordings show the woman tried to drive away slowly while officers pulled at her car door. An officer then fired shots, and the car crashed. The event caused anger among local people and leaders. The national government defended the officer. The president said the woman acted dangerously and claimed the officer shot in self-defense . The Department of Homeland Security said the woman used her car as a weapon and called her a domestic terrorist. Allegedly, the woman had harassed officers all day prior to the shooting. Officials said the officer feared for his life and followed his training. The city mayor strongly rejected this view after watching the video. He said officers recklessly used force and told immigration agents to leave the city. Many people now debate what really happened. Videos spread online, and different sides see the same images in very different ways. Difficult words: self-defense (protecting yourself when someone tries to hurt you), prior to (before something happens), reckless ly (in a dangerous way without thinking). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Immigration officers shot and killed a woman during a raid in Minneapolis, US. The officers stopped her car and told her to get out. Videos show her trying to drive away slowly while officers pulled the door. An officer then shot her, and the car crashed. Many people in the city feel angry and shocked. The president and government leaders defend the officer. They say the woman tried to hurt officers with her car. They say the officer feared for his life and wanted to protect himself and others. The government calls the woman dangerous. The boss of Minneapolis got very angry. He said the officer used power in a dangerous way and asked immigration officers to leave the city. People online watch the same videos but have very different opinions. The event made people talk again about immigration and safety. Difficult words: immigration officer (a government worker who controls who can enter or stay in a country), raid (a quick police action), defend (to protect someone or say they are right). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Immigration officers stop a woman in her car in Minneapolis, US. They tell her to get out. In videos, the woman tries to drive away slowly. An officer shoots her. The car hits another car. People feel shocked and angry. The president says that the officer only wants to be safe. Officials say that the woman tries to hurt officers with her car. They say that the officer does the right thing. The boss of the city is very angry. He says that the officer uses power in a bad way. He tells immigration officers to leave the city. People watch videos online and think different things. Many people talk about immigration. They want to be safe. Difficult words: immigration officer (an official who checks who comes into a country), shocked (very surprised and upset), power (when you are strong enough to make things happen). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Food waste is a serious global problem, and it adds strongly to global warming. When people throw food away, it often goes to landfills . There, food breaks down and releases methane, a gas that heats the planet much more than carbon dioxide. When people burn food waste, it releases large amounts of carbon dioxide because food contains a lot of water. Scientists say food waste causes about eight to ten percent of all greenhouse gas output in the world. This amount is higher than emissions from many large countries. Studies show that people waste food at many stages. Waste happens in homes and shops, but also on farms and during transport. New research suggests the real amount of wasted food is much higher than earlier reports. In poorer areas, farmers often lack storage or transport, so food rots before people can buy it. This waste also means a waste of land, energy, and work. Experts say food waste is a chance to act. Better storage, smaller food packs, and simple local solutions can cut waste. Reducing food waste can lower emissions and help feed more people without using more land. Difficult words: landfill (a place where people put trash in the ground), output (the amount something produces), lack (to not have enough of something), rot (go bad and break down). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Throwing away food is a big problem for the planet. When people throw food away, it often goes to landfills . There, food creates methane, a gas which heats the Earth much more than carbon dioxide. Burning food waste also creates a lot of carbon dioxide because food holds water. Experts say food waste creates about eight to ten percent of global gas which warms the planet. People throw away food everywhere. Families waste food at home, shops throw food away, and farms lose food too. New studies show farms waste much more food than people first thought. In many countries, farmers don’t have cold storage , so food gets bad before it reaches buyers. Experts say people can solve this problem. Better storage, smaller food packs, and simple changes can help. When people waste less food, they protect the planet and save land, energy, and work. Difficult words: landfill (a place where people put trash), waste (to throw away or not use), storage (a place to keep things). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Food waste is a big problem for the planet. People throw food away every day. Much of this food goes to landfills . There, food makes gas, which makes the world warmer. Burning food waste also makes bad gas called carbon dioxide. Food waste makes the world warmer. Food waste happens in many places. Families throw away food, and shops too. Farms throw away food, too. Many farmers do not have cold places to keep food. The food goes bad fast. This means people lose food and work. People can solve this problem. Better food storage helps. You should buy only what you need. When people throw away less food, they save land, water, energy, and work. Difficult words: waste (what you throw away because you do not need it anymore), landfill (a place where people put things which they do not want anymore), storage (a place to keep things). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Denmark was one of the first countries to use digital tools in schools and public life. Children have used tablets, digital books, and phones for many years. However, new data shows that too much screen time harms children’s mental health and school results. Many teenagers spend over five hours a day on their phones. Experts say this reduces focus , learning, and time with other people. Because of this, Denmark now changes direction . Schools across the country ban mobile phones during lessons and breaks. Children place phones in locked boxes at the start of the day. Paper books return to classrooms, and teachers use computers only under control. Youth clubs and sports groups also ban phones. Adults notice better focus, more energy, and stronger social contact when phones are put away. The government also plans limits on social media use for young people. A proposal aims to ban social media for children under fifteen, and many parents and groups support this change. Denmark hopes these steps help children grow more healthily and calmly. Difficult words: focus (to pay full attention to something), direction (the way someone or something is moving or changing), aim (a goal or something you want to achieve). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Denmark used digital tools in schools for many years. Children used phones, tablets, and screens every day. New studies show this harms mental health and learning. Many teens spend more than five hours a day on phones. Teachers see problems with focus and social life. Because of this, Denmark is now changing its rules. Schools ban mobile phones during school time. Children put phones in locked boxes each morning. Paper books return to classrooms, and teachers control computer use. Clubs and sports places also ban phones. Children say they feel calmer and talk more with others. The country also plans to make rules for social media. A new plan may stop children under fifteen from using social media. Parents and experts support this idea. Denmark wants to protect children and help them grow better. Difficult words: mental health (how your mind and feelings are, like being happy or stressed), focus (to look at one thing, or to think about one thing for some time), ban (an official no to something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Denmark uses many digital tools in the past. Children use phones and screens at school. Now adults see problems. Children feel stressed. They cannot think clearly. Many children use phones for five hours a day. This is bad for learning and health. Children in schools now cannot use their phones. They give phones to teachers each morning. Paper books return to class. Clubs and sports places also stop using phones. Children talk more and play more together. Denmark also plans new rules. Children under fifteen may not use social media. Parents and teachers are happy with this change. They want children to be healthy and happy. Difficult words: digital tool (a computer, phone, or app), adult (a person who is not a child anymore), healthy (when you feel well and your body and mind are okay). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Elvis Presley fans and tribute artists started their yearly trip to a famous music festival in a small town in Australia. They met at a main train station in Sydney and traveled 357 kilometers on the Elvis Express, a special train made for the event. Many fans wore Elvis clothes and enjoyed music on the long journey. The seven-hour trip offered shows and live music from tribute artists who performed well-known Elvis songs. One singer from the UK said he decided to join the festival after people had told him how special it felt. He said Elvis’ music brought joy and helped people feel calm during hard times. The festival takes place every January and brings a very large crowd to the town. Organizers expect about 24,000 visitors, which is double the number of local people. For many fans, the event offers happiness, music, and a break from daily stress . Difficult words: tribute (show of respect), crowd (a large group of people in one place), stress (strong worry). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Elvis Presley fans traveled from Sydney to a small town for a yearly music festival . They went by the Elvis Express, a special train for the event. Fans wore Elvis clothes and enjoyed music together during the long trip. The train ride lasted seven hours and offered shows with singers who performed famous Elvis songs. One singer from the UK said he chose to come after friends told him good things about the festival. He said Elvis’ music brought joy and helped people forget problems. The festival happens every January and brings many visitors to the town. This year, about 24,000 people came to the event. This number is much higher than the number of people who live there. Fans come to feel happy and enjoy music. Difficult words: festival (a big event for many people), perform (to sing, play music, or act in front of people), joy (a happy feeling). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Elvis Presley fans go by train from Sydney to a small town in Australia. The train has the name Elvis Express. People wear Elvis clothes and listen to music on the trip . The train trip lasts seven hours. Singers perform famous Elvis songs. One singer comes from the UK. He feels happy at the festival. Elvis’ music gives people good feelings. It makes them calm . They stop thinking about everyday problems. The festival happens every January. Many people visit the town for this event. About 24,000 people come. Fans enjoy music and feel happy. Difficult words: trip (when you travel from one place to another), perform (to sing, play music, or act in front of people), calm (a quiet feeling). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A family walk and picnic in the Dolomites, Italy, was interrupted by a shocking and unexpected encounter with a bear. Twelve-year-old Alessandro was wandering among the bushes looking for pine cones , when he appeared to be followed by a bear. The boy, who is passionate about nature, knew that he had to walk away slowly not to alarm the animal. Alessandro’s mother panicked; however, the boy told her to be silent. When he safely reached his family, the bear stopped following him and disappeared. Later, Alessandro told the local press that the secret was to keep calm and not to look the animal in the eyes. He also revealed that he was so excited about the adventure, and that he was the happiest child in the world. Difficult words: encounter (an unexpected meeting), cone (the dry brown fruit of a tree such as a pine or a fir), reveal (to make something public information). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

A family made a trip to the Dolomites, Italy. They were having a picnic, and twelve-year-old Alessandro was wandering in the bushes. Suddenly, a bear appeared behind him, and the animal started to move towards the boy. Alessando is very keen on nature, and he knew that he had to walk slowly away. If the boy walked too fast, the bear could attack him. It was also important not to look the bear in the eyes. Alessandro’s mother was very scared, and the boy told her to stay calm. When the boy reached his family, the bear went away. Later, Alessandro said that the experience was very exciting. The boy said that he was the happiest child in the world. Difficult words: keen (be very interested, like something very much), reach (to get to a place or close to someone), experience (something that happens to someone). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A family makes a trip to the mountains. The mountains are in Italy. The family is having a picnic. A boy is playing in the bushes . The boy’s name is Alessandro. He is 12 years old. Alessandro’s father is filming the boy on his phone. Suddenly, a bear appears behind the boy. The bear starts to come closer to the boy. Alessandro slowly walks away from the bear. The bear follows the boy. Alessandro’s mother is very scared. The boy tells her to stay calm. The boy loves nature. He knows a lot of information. He knows that he must not look in the bear’s eyes. The boy gets to his parents. The bear goes away. Alessandro is excited about the bear. He says that he is the happiest child in the world. Difficult words: bush (a plant that looks like a small tree, and it often grows in mountains), appear (to show up), excited (when someone feels very happy about something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

From 1 January 2026, imports of steel, aluminium, cement, and similar goods to the European Union have to pay a new carbon border tax. The rule links the price of imports to the CO2 released during production. The EU says this step protects European companies that already face strict climate rules and helps keep competition fair. Importers have to buy certificates that match the carbon level of the goods, with prices close to the EU carbon market. The new tax has caused strong reactions outside the EU. The United States, China, India, Russia, and South Africa say the law hurts trade and acts like protectionism . Some countries question if the rule follows World Trade Organization rules. The US already raised tariffs on EU goods and warned about more trade conflict. The EU says the tax will push cleaner production around the world and stop companies from moving to countries with weaker rules. The EU also plans to use part of the tax money to support its industries during this change. Difficult words: competition (when people or companies try to do better than others to win customers or success), protectionism (when a country makes rules to protect its own businesses from foreign companies), tariff (a tax a country adds to goods coming from other countries). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

From January 2026, companies that bring steel, aluminium, and cement into the EU must pay for the carbon these goods create. The EU says this rule protects European companies and keeps competition fair. European companies must buy special certificates with the carbon level of the goods. Many countries disagree with the new rule. The United States, China, India, Russia, and South Africa say it hurts trade and is good only for the EU. Some countries fear more trade problems, especially after the US raised tariffs on EU products. The EU says the tax supports cleaner production and stops companies from moving to countries with weaker climate rules. The EU also plans to use some of the money from the tax to help its own industries deal with higher costs. Difficult words: cement (a gray powder to make walls, roads, and other structures), competition (when people or companies try to do better than others), tariff (a tax on things from other countries). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The EU says that this helps European companies and keeps rules fair. Some countries do not agree with the rule, for example, the United States, China, or India. They say that it is bad for business. They worry about more problems in the future. The EU says that the tax helps the planet. It makes production clean. The EU also wants to use the money to help its own companies. Difficult words: carbon tax (money which companies pay for the carbon gas they produce, to help the planet), agree (to say yes), production (making things). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

In a video shared by the British Transport Police, an unknown man can be seen pushing between barriers at Brimsdown Level Crossing, Hertfordshire. After forcing his way through the gate, the man casually makes his way onto the tracks, making it across just in time as a train whizzes past. When the man reaches the other side, he glances left, and he very narrowly avoids being hit by the train. In a statement, officials said that the man’s reckless behavior could have cost him his life. Officials also pointed out that the warning signs, barriers, and flashing lights are there for a reason. Some trains travel at high speeds, and a train, that a person thinks is in the distance, could be close within seconds. Difficult words: whiz (to move quickly through the air or on the ground), glance (to take a quick look at something), reckless (doing something dangerous and not worrying about the risks). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

The British Transport Police shared a video of an unknown man at a railway crossing in Hertfordshire. The man pushed through the gate, walked across the tracks, and glanced left. At the same moment, a train came, and it almost hit the man. When the train left, the man slowly walked away. Officials say that the man’s behavior was very dangerous, and he nearly lost his life. People must respect the warning signs and flashing lights, and they must not push through the barriers. Some trains travel very fast. They can seem far away; however, they can be close in a few seconds. Difficult words: railway crossing (a place where a railway and a road cross), glance (to look at something quickly), flashing (when lights turn on and off quickly so you can see them easily and from far away). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Many people feel pressure to share their lives online to show success and purpose. However, some of the strongest people choose privacy instead. They don’t post often, and they don’t look for attention . This choice brings more peace and clear thinking. Silence doesn’t mean fear or weakness; it usually shows trust in oneself and steady personal growth. These people don’t need approval from others. They don’t explain every part of their life or turn personal moments into public posts. Their progress stays private because it matters to them. They trust their own opinion and feel comfortable with who they are. Real confidence doesn’t ask for approval and doesn’t need noise to feel strong. These people also trade attention for peace. They focus on real work and clear goals. They follow their own path and protect their energy. Privacy becomes a limit that gives strength when they choose to speak or appear. Difficult words: pressure (a strong feeling to do something), attention (when people look at you or think about what you do), approval (agreement or praise from others). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

They don’t explain their life online or show every success. They trust themselves and feel good without likes or comments. They focus on what is important to them and don’t need approval to feel strong. These people choose peace over attention; they focus on work and growth. They protect their energy and share only with people who matter. Staying offline helps them grow and stay strong. Difficult words: attention (when people look at you or think about what you do), confidence (belief in yourself), approval (when someone says yes to something or shows they like it). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The US President Donald Trump ordered air strikes on military sites inside Venezuela, including targets in the capital city. US officials confirmed this action. People in the city reported loud explosions, strong sounds, and shaking homes. Smoke rose above the city, and many residents felt fear and confusion . After the strikes, the city became quiet; however, people continued to contact family and friends to check their safety. The Venezuelan government strongly rejected the attack. Officials said the US wanted oil and other resources. They asked the international community to act and requested a meeting of the Security Council. The government declared a national emergency, but its public message appeared unclear and weak. Military experts said Venezuela had little ability to resist such an attack. Trump said US forces seized President Nicolas Maduro and his wife and flew them to New York. Maduro faces drug and weapons charges. Trump said the US would control Venezuela for a time and warned about a larger attack if needed. Difficult words: confusion (a state when people do not understand what is happening), resist (to try to stop or fight against something), seize (to take a person or thing by force). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Difficult words: air strike (an attack from the air, usually by planes), explosion (a very loud blast), reject (to say no to something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A large bank robbery shocked Germany after thieves stole valuables worth tens of millions of euros from a bank in a western city. Police say the robbers drilled through a thick basement wall to reach the vault . Firefighters discovered the crime after a fire alarm rang, but they found no fire, only a hole and an empty vault. Many customers rushed to the bank in fear and anger. Most safety boxes were opened, and people worry that their losses go beyond insurance limits . Some lost family gold and jewelry with deep personal value. Police believe the robbers used a nearby parking garage and planned the crime very carefully. Investigators see signs of an organized crime group. Experts say inside information may help explain how the thieves avoided alarms. Police search for suspects among current or former staff and security workers. No arrests have happened, and the thieves remain free. Difficult words: vault (a secure room for money and expensive things), insurance limit (the highest amount of money an insurance company will pay for a loss or damage), avoid (to stay away from something or do something). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Customers came to the bank very upset and afraid. Most safety boxes were open, and many people feared they would lose more than the bank could give them back. Some jewelry had strong family meaning, such as old coins and rings. Police say the crime shows strong planning and teamwork. Experts believe the robbers may know the bank systems well. Officers now look at staff and security workers for possible help. No one is under arrest, and police continue their search. Difficult words: worth (how much money something has), drill (a tool to make holes), vault (a room for money and expensive things). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Bulgaria becomes the 21st country to use the euro on New Year’s Day, which marks an important step in its connection with the EU. Many businesses support the change because it makes trade easier, especially for companies that work with partners in other countries. They no longer need to exchange money, which saves time and cost and helps cross-border business grow. However, many people feel worried about the new currency . Prices already rise due to inflation , and many citizens fear the euro will make daily life more expensive. Political problems add to this concern , since recent protests removed the government from power. Analysts say leaders don’t explain the change well enough, which leaves people unsure about what to expect. Older people, people in remote areas, and people with less education may face the most trouble at first. Some political parties also don’t agree with the euro because they fear a loss of national identity. Even though experts expect only short price changes, almost half of Bulgarians still don’t want the euro. Difficult words: curr ency (a type of money), inflation (a rise in prices), concern (a worry or something that makes you feel worried), remote (far away from cities or main places). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Inflation already affects daily life, and people are afraid the euro will raise costs even more. Recent protests also created political problems, and experts say the government doesn’t explain the change clearly. Older people and people who don’t live in cities may find the change hard. Some political groups don’t like the euro because they worry about losing Bulgarian culture. Almost half of Bulgarians don’t want the euro, even though experts say that prices will go up only for some time. Difficult words: currency (a type of money), foreign (from another country), inflation (when prices go up). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Many people say no to the euro, even when experts say price changes stay small. Difficult words: cost (money which you need to buy something), rise (to go up), culture (the way of life of people). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

David Fear, a senior film critic at Rolling Stone, presents the five best films from 2025. Fifth, Richard Linklater’s Nouvelle Vague explores the world of the French New Wave and serves as an exciting cinematic team-up for fans of film history. Clint Bentley’s Train Dreams follows at number four, and offers a beautifully crafted adaptation of Denis Johnson’s novella that tells an epic story from the early twentieth century. Robert Grainier, a railroad worker, lives a quiet life until he marries and has a daughter. Steven Soderbergh’s Black Bag takes the third spot. It is a spy drama where a top British intelligence agent must find a mole leaking classified software. Number two is Chloe Zhao’s Hamnet , which uses the novel by Maggie O’Farrell. The historical drama depicts the tragedy of William Shakespeare’s son and the emotional strength of his wife, Agnes. It illustrates how personal pain can lead to artistic healing and catharsis . The top film of 2025 is Paul Thomas Anderson’s latest work, One Battle After Another . It captures the complex feelings of living in modern America and suggests that the best way to handle a broken world is to focus on love. Difficult words: team-up (an occasion when two or more people or characters work together to achieve something), novella (a short book), catharsis (releasing strong emotions through art). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Difficult words: film critic (a person who watches movies and tells people if they are good or bad), spy (a person who gets secret information about someone, a business, or another country), tragedy (a very sad event or situation). Many people set goals for the new year, but most stop after a short time. Studies show that only a small number of people reach their resolutions . Psychotherapist Lisa Palmer explains that this often happens because people try to change actions without changing how they think. She says mindset plays a key role in success. When people believe they are capable and worthy , goals feel more possible and less stressful. Palmer advises people to start with small and realistic steps. Goals should match personal values and life purpose. She explains that motivation grows when people feel supported, sometimes with coaching or professional help. Mistakes will happen, but failure doesn’t mean the goal is lost. Pro gress comes from standing up again and learning what works better next time. She also stresses kindness toward oneself. People should accept imperfect days, focus on strengths, and try new methods instead of repeating old habits. Palmer says that positive thinking, health, happiness, and presence in daily life make long-term success easier to achieve. Difficult words: resolution (a clear decision or promise to change or do something), worthy (good enough to deserve respect, care, or success), progress (slow movement forward or improvement). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Many people make New Year’s goals, but most quit after a few weeks. An expert explains that people fail because they focus only on actions and not on thinking. She says a strong mindset helps people believe they can change and succeed . She tells people to choose small and clear goals. Goals should fit the person and feel meaningful. A coach or therapist can help you stay focused and motivated. When people make mistakes, they should not give up. They can learn and try again in a new way. Palmer also says people need to be kind to themselves. Everyone has bad days, but positive thinking helps people stay calm and keep moving forward. When people care about their health and stay happy, goals feel easier to reach. Difficult words: fail (to not reach a goal or not succeed), mindset (the way a person thinks and sees situations), succeed (to reach a goal or do something well). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.
